newsitem.title: UK: UK raises rates, boosts central bank independence.
newsitem.headline: UK raises rates, boosts central bank independence.

text.p: Britain's new Labour government astounded financial markets on Tuesday by announcing that it would give the Bank of England freedom to set interest rates.

Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Gordon Brown raised interest rates to 6.25 percent from 6.0 percent to prevent inflation getting out of hand -- but declared that his first monetary decision would also be his last.

"We must remove the suspicion that short-term party-political considerations are influencing the setting of interest rates," he told his first news conference since Labour's landslide election victory on May 1.
"I have therefore decided to give the Bank of England operational responsibility for setting interest rates, with immediate effect."
Brown's dramatic decision to relinquish one of his key powers sent London share prices rocketing, while sterling firmed to a four-and-a-half year high against the deutschemark.
British government bond prices also surged and the "spread" over German bonds -- the premium investors demand before they will lend Britain money in preference to Germany -- narrowed sharply.
However, economists said the decision did not satisfy the criteria for joining a single European currency.

"The Bank has to be made entirely independent and the government has retained its right to issue instructions," said Graham Bishop, adviser on European financial affairs at Salomon Brothers. "This is a building block, a launch pad."
Brown told the news conference it was unlikely that Britain would be an EMU member in the first wave due to start in 1999.
Until now, Chancellors have set monetary policy after hearing the advice of the Bank of England.

Bank Governor Eddie George had been calling for higher interest rates since December, but Conservative Chancellor Kenneth Clarke had rejected his advice, prompting accusations that he did not want to risk upsetting voters ahead of the election by making home loans more expensive.

Clarke described the decision as "unwise and precipitate" and said Brown would come to regret it. "What you are going to see is, undoubtedly, tighter monetary policy than you might otherwise have," he told BBC Radio.
Brown's reforms went much further than those he had outlined before the election, when he said he would not propose early operational independence for the Bank.

"We will only build a fully credible framework for monetary policy if the long-term needs of the economy, not short-term political considerations, guide monetary decision-making," Brown said on Tuesday.
"I want Britain's economic success to be built on the solid rock of prudent and consistent economic management, not the shifting sands of boom and bust."
"This is the time to set the British economy on a new long-term course that will deliver high levels of growth and employment through lasting stability."

The new chancellor, who had promised he would "hit the ground running," said he had decided to raise interest rates because of rapid growth in consumer spending and average earnings, rising house prices and strong growth in money supply.
"My judgement is that we have inherited a situation in which, in the absence of corrective action, inflation will overshoot the government's inflation target next year," he said.

Labour has adopted the target of 2.5 percent or less for underlying inflation set by the previous government. The underlying annual rate, excluding volatile mortgage interest payments, was 2.7 percent in March.

Commercial banks followed the move by raising their base lending rates to 6.25 percent while the Halifax Building Society, the country's largest mortgage lender, raised its rate on home loans to 7.6 percent from 7.25 percent.
Brown said he aimed to break the boom-bust cycles that had hobbled Britain's economic performance for decades.
"The enemy of growth and the investment necessary for it is the instability of short periodic bursts of high growth followed by recession," Brown said.
Interest rates will in future be set at a monthly meeting of a new nine-member monetary policy committee, including four members from outside the Bank of England.
The government will continue to set the inflation target, leaving the Bank free to set interest rates to achieve it.
